L’Europa, vistosamente assente dalla top 5, continua a pagare il prezzo di una frammentazione normativa e di una crescita anemica 📉 che penalizza la competitività dei suoi campioni bancari sulla scena internazionale.

È un po’ la fotografia dei mercati: scosse continue, ma niente “crash” pulito 📉. Da una parte tassi ancora alti più a lungo e rendimenti che tengono il mercato sotto pressione. Dall’altra utili che non stanno collassando e un’economia che, fin qui, resta più resistente del previsto 📊.

In mezzo c’è la grande variabile 2026: l’AI 🤖. Non tanto l’hype, quanto la domanda vera che sta facendo impazzire gli investitori: “tutto questo capex genererà ritorni?” 💸 Quando la risposta è incerta, anche i titoli migliori diventano nervosi e basta poco per far partire prese di profitto.

Per questo vedi giornate in cui sembra che “si rompa tutto” ⚡, e poi il mercato si ricompone: rotazione tra settori (non solo tech), ricerca di qualità, difesa su chi è troppo caro, caccia a chi è rimasto indietro 🔄.

Il punto, oggi, non è cercare il minimo o il massimo 🎯. È capire se si sta deteriorando la base: margini, flussi di cassa, accesso al credito. Finché questi tengono, la volatilità è rumore, non rottura strutturale. 🧠

.

#Nabila #finanza #economia #nabilafinanza #educazionefinanziaria

Nel breve periodo il mercato è rumoroso, emotivo, imprevedibile 📉. È qui che il rischio appare più alto, perché i prezzi riflettono aspettative, paure, cicli economici e shock temporanei ⚡️.
 Nel lungo periodo, però, l’azione rappresenta una cosa molto diversa: una quota di un’attività reale, che produce utili, reinveste capitale, innova e cresce insieme all’economia 🏭.

Valutare il rischio solo in termini numerici significa ignorare fattori fondamentali: il tempo, la qualità del business, la solidità dei flussi di cassa, la capacità di adattarsi ai cambiamenti, il contesto macroeconomico e l’impatto dell’inflazione ⏳.
 Un prezzo che oscilla non è automaticamente un rischio, se il valore sottostante continua a crescere e a generare redditività nel tempo 📊.

Nel lungo termine, cioè su orizzonti temporali estesi, i mercati azionari hanno quasi sempre restituito rendimenti positivi, proprio perché riflettono la crescita economica, l’aumento della produttività e la capacità delle imprese di creare valore nel tempo 🚀.

Il vero rischio, nel lungo periodo, non è la volatilità, ma la perdita permanente di capitale o l’erosione del potere d’acquisto 🧠.

Il brusco crollo di oro e argento non è stato casuale, né puramente tecnico ⚠️. 

Il catalizzatore è arrivato dalla politica monetaria: la nomina di Kevin Warsh alla presidenza della Federal Reserve ha ridisegnato in poche ore le aspettative degli investitori 🏦.

Dopo un rally record alimentato da tensioni geopolitiche, timori sull’indipendenza della Fed e forte domanda speculativa, i metalli preziosi hanno perso uno dei loro principali sostegni: l’idea di una banca centrale più accomodante. Warsh è percepito come una figura ortodossa, attenta alla credibilità istituzionale e meno incline a tollerare deviazioni sull’inflazione 📉.

Lunedì le vendite si sono intensificate, aggravando le perdite del venerdì precedente. L’oro spot ha ceduto circa il 5%, scendendo a 4.616 dollari l’oncia, dopo il crollo di quasi -10% di venerdì, quando i prezzi erano scivolati sotto quota 5.000 dollari 💰.

Ancora più violenta la correzione dell’argento: il metallo è crollato di oltre il 30% nella giornata di venerdì, registrando la peggior seduta dal marzo 1980 🔥.

A esacerbare il movimento hanno contribuito l’elevata leva, l’aumento dei requisiti di margine e la riduzione forzata delle posizioni più affollate. In mercati iper-sensibili alle aspettative, non è il dato macro a fare la differenza, ma il cambio di narrativa 🧠.

Per molti investitori l’immobiliare rappresenta una sorta di rifugio mentale 🧠. 

Un bene che “si vede”, che si tocca, che dà l’illusione di controllo 🧱. Ma nei patrimoni reali, quelli che crescono e resistono nel tempo ⏳, la casa non è mai solo una casa: è una decisione finanziaria con effetti profondi.

Il mattone può offrire stabilità, reddito e protezione dall’inflazione 🏠, ma introduce anche rigidità. Capitale immobilizzato, scarsa flessibilità, esposizione geografica concentrata. Ogni scelta immobiliare lega il patrimonio a un territorio, a una fiscalità, a una dinamica demografica precisa. E quando lo scenario cambia, adattarsi non è immediato.

Chi guarda il patrimonio in modo evoluto sa che il vero rischio non è la volatilità, ma l’inefficienza ⚖️. Avere troppo capitale fermo, rinunciare a opportunità, perdere la possibilità di ribilanciare nel tempo. Per questo l’immobiliare funziona solo se inserito in una strategia più ampia, dove dialoga con asset liquidi, strumenti finanziari e obiettivi di lungo periodo.

La differenza non la fa il singolo investimento, ma il disegno complessivo. È questa la logica con cui operano multi family office come cunibertipartners , che affiancano famiglie e imprenditori nella lettura del patrimonio come sistema, aiutandoli a trasformare scelte isolate in una strategia coerente, solida e sostenibile nel tempo 📊.

The World Map Lies: Why the Map You Learned Is Wrong

The world map you grew up seeing may not represent the true size of countries.

The famous Mercator projection, created in 1569, was designed to represent the round Earth on a flat surface. But as you move toward the poles, landmasses become increasingly stretched. That is why Greenland can appear enormous compared with Africa—even though Africa is vastly larger.

A newer projection, Equal Earth, presents a much more accurate comparison of land areas. Africa, South America and South Asia appear closer to their actual proportions, while Europe, North America and Russia lose the exaggerated size they have on Mercator maps.

The debate has now reached the global stage, raising a bigger question: Are maps ever truly neutral?

This isn’t just about geography. Maps influence how we visualize countries, continents and global power.

Why it matters for your index fund: the more the government pays to borrow, the harder it is for stocks to compete. Next month's five-year auction is the test.

Meta just had its best month in thirteen years. Thirty-six percent, in September alone. And you’re probably reading this on one of its apps.

Going into the month, Meta had gone nowhere for a year: the stock was down about 5% over twelve months, and in mid-August it was one of the worst performers in the S&P 500. The market had decided the company was spending too much on AI and getting too little back. Then it launched Muse, its new AI assistant, which hit number one on Apple’s App Store within days. On September 21 the stock jumped 11% in a single day, and by the end of the week Meta was within 1% of a $2 trillion market cap, up 43% from its August low.

The last time Meta had a month like this was July 2013, when it was still called Facebook and had just proven it could make money on phones. The whole company was worth about $90 billion then. This month, the same kind of move added roughly half a trillion.

Why does a stock sit flat for a year and then move in thirty days? Because prices don’t move on time, they move when the story changes. For a year the story was “expensive AI, no proof.” One product hit number one and the story flipped, and everyone who’d been waiting for proof bought at once. If you own an index fund you were in it: Meta is roughly 3% of the S&P 500, so this one company added about a percentage point to your index this month.

Honest caveat: in 2013 the rally came with a business that had already proven itself. This one comes with a plan to spend around $140 billion this year. A month like this says the story changed. It doesn’t say the story is finished.

Two companies are now fifteen percent of the entire S&P 500. That has never happened, not even at the peak of the dot-com bubble.

The index holds five hundred companies, but as of this week Apple and Nvidia together make up more than 15% of it. The old record was set in 2000, at the top of the bubble, when Microsoft and General Electric combined for 9.1%. Today’s pair beats that by more than five points. Nvidia alone is worth about $5.4 trillion, while the smallest company in the same index is one hundredth of one percent, roughly eight hundred times smaller by weight.

It happens because the S&P 500 is weighted by size. The bigger a company gets, the bigger its slice, so when a stock wins, index funds buy more of it automatically. Winners grow their own weight. And since most 401(k)s and index funds track this exact list, fifteen cents of every dollar you have in “the market” is really in two companies. Earlier this year the top ten alone were 36% of the index, versus 23% in 2000. Diversified doesn’t mean what it meant twenty years ago.

Honest caveat: this isn’t a bubble call. In 2000 the giants were priced on hype; today these two earn a huge share of the index’s actual profits, and concentration can stay high for years. A record tells you where you are, not what happens next.

Everyone is asking whether World War Three is coming. Here’s what wars have actually done to the stock market: the average war shock cost stocks 5%. A normal year costs 14%.

Researchers tracked about 25 major geopolitical shocks since World War Two. On the day of the event the S&P 500 fell about 1%. From peak to bottom, 5% on average. Nineteen days to hit the bottom, 42 days to recover everything. Even Pearl Harbor followed the pattern: a 20% fall, ten months to recover, and stocks higher by the end of the war than the day it began. The largest conflict in human history was a bad year for stocks, not a lost decade.

The strange part: the rumor is often worse than the event. Markets spent months dreading the 2003 invasion of Iraq, and the day it began, the market went up 8% in the first month. Uncertainty is what markets hate. A war starting is at least a certainty.

What actually decides the damage is oil. The two worst wars for stocks were oil wars: 1973 at minus 16%, Kuwait in 1990 at minus 17%. 9/11 recovered in a month, Ukraine in three weeks. An oil shock becomes inflation, inflation becomes higher rates, and higher rates are what hurt stocks. This year proved it exactly: stocks fell 9% when the Iran conflict began and recovered, but oil past $100 pushed inflation up, the Fed hiked, and yields hit 5%. The war didn’t hurt stocks directly. The barrel did.

Honest caveat: every event in this data was contained. A direct war between nuclear powers has no row in the table, and anyone claiming to know what that would do is guessing. Wars during recessions behaved much worse. History is a guide, not a guarantee.

If you’re watching the headlines for the market, watch the barrel instead.

Every single night, Wall Street borrows around three trillion dollars. It pays it all back by morning, then does it again. It’s the biggest market you’ve never heard of.

It’s called the repo market, and it’s basically a pawn shop for Wall Street: a bank hands over a government bond as collateral, gets cash for the night, and buys the bond back tomorrow for slightly more. That tiny difference is the interest. Banks, hedge funds and dealers all need cash to hold positions overnight, and the lenders are largely money market funds, which means if you keep cash in one, you’re a lender in this market tonight.

Three trillion a night is just the slice the Fed measures for its benchmark rate. Count every corner and the Fed puts overnight repo above eight trillion dollars a day. The entire stock market trades about one.

It’s invisible because it’s plumbing, and plumbing only makes the news when it breaks. On September 17, 2019, the cash ran short and the overnight rate more than doubled in a day, touching 10% intraday with nothing wrong in the economy. The Fed injected tens of billions the next morning. And in March 2008, Bear Stearns lost its overnight funding in days and was gone by the weekend, not because it lost money that week, but because the lenders stopped rolling the loans.

The overnight repo rate now underpins over $200 trillion of loans, mortgages and derivatives. When you hear “the Fed injected liquidity,” this is the pipe. It’s not a conspiracy, it’s infrastructure. The stock market is the show. The repo market is the electricity.

Had you ever heard of the repo market before this?

The worst day in stock market history happened in a year the market finished up. One day: minus 22.6%. The year: positive.

October 19, 1987. No war had started, no bank had failed, no recession was coming — and the Dow fell 22.6% in a single session, roughly half a trillion dollars gone in six and a half hours. Nearly double the crash of 1929, and nothing has come close since. The cause, for the first time ever, was machines: portfolio insurance programs coded to sell automatically as prices fell. Prices fell, computers sold, the selling pushed prices lower, so the computers sold more. A doom loop at machine speed.

The next morning the Federal Reserve released one sentence — it would supply whatever liquidity the system needed — and the panic stopped. The market rose almost 6% that day, recovered over half the crash within two days, finished 1987 positive, and was back at record highs within two years. The recession everyone braced for never came. The only permanent mark: circuit breakers, invented the following year, still protecting every session today.

Who actually lost money? Not the market. The people who sold into the panic. The worst day in history was survivable. Panicking on it wasn’t.

Honest caveat: not every crash resolves this gently — 2008 came with a real recession attached. The lesson isn’t that crashes don’t matter. It’s that the day itself tells you nothing.

The average house has barely beaten inflation for over a hundred years. The same money in stocks became fifteen times more, just since 1988.

“Safe as houses” is the one piece of financial advice every family passes down, and nobody ever checks the number. The amount of money where work becomes optional is one multiplication. Your yearly spending, times twenty-five.

Spend $40,000 a year and your number is $1 million. Spend $60,000 and it’s $1.5 million. Notice it’s based on your spending, not your income.

This isn’t a rule of thumb, it’s a study. In 1994, William Bengen tested every retirement date since 1926, including someone retiring straight into the 1929 crash and someone retiring into the brutal 1970s, and asked what withdrawal rate survived them all. The answer: 4% a year, adjusted for inflation. And 4% flipped around is 25x. The Trinity Study later put the success rate at 95% over thirty-year retirements with half the portfolio in stocks, through depressions and crashes.

The multiplication cuts both ways: every dollar of yearly spending costs $25 of freedom. Cut $1,000 a year from your lifestyle and your number drops by $25,000. Spending less isn’t just saving money, it’s shrinking the finish line.

Honest caveat: this number is being fought over right now. Morningstar says 3.9%, Bengen himself now says 4.7%, and very early retirees should use closer to 3.5%. It’s a guideline built on history, not a guarantee, and it assumes an invested portfolio with a large share in stocks.

So do the multiplication. Your yearly spending, times twenty-five. What’s your number?

One investor timed the market perfectly for twenty straight years. He beat the investor with no strategy at all by nine percent. And the one who waited for the perfect moment lost to everybody, even the unluckiest.

Twenty years of perfect foresight was worth about $15,000. The unluckiest investor made triple the careful one. The only strategy that lost was waiting. Waiting for the dip sounds like a strategy. It’s just cash with a story attached.

Honest caveat: this window includes big bull years and the gaps shrink in weaker eras, but the ranking held in every window Schwab tested back to 1926.

The market barely punishes bad timing. It brutally punishes no timing.

Held for one day, the stock market is a coin flip. Held for twenty years, it has never lost. Not once.

Since 1926, the market went up on just 53% of days — barely better than random. But change one variable, how long you hold, and everything transforms. One year: about 75% of periods positive. Five years: 88%. Ten years: 94%. And twenty years: researchers checked all 864 rolling windows since 1926, and losses were zero. Even someone who bought in 1928, directly before the worst crash in history, made money over the following twenty years. The worst possible timing still won.

Why? In the short run, prices follow moods — fear, greed, headlines, noise. Underneath it all, companies keep earning, and earnings grow over years, not days. Hold long enough and the noise cancels out. What’s left is the growth.

Honest caveat: 100% describes the past, it doesn’t command the future. And the worst twenty-year stretch made money barely. Time raises your odds. It doesn’t delete risk.

The market doesn’t pay you for being smart or for timing. It pays you for staying long enough for the coin flip to become a certainty. Risk has an expiration date.

Almost every single year, the stock market crashes. And almost every single year, it finishes up anyway.

From its high to its low, the market’s average drop inside a calendar year is 14%. Every year, like clockwork. JPMorgan tracked it back to 1980: forty-six years, an average intra-year fall of 14.2%, and yet 35 of those 46 years finished positive, with the average year ending up about 10%. The scary number and the good number came from the exact same years.

2020 is the extreme case: a 34% collapse in a single month, and the year still finished up. And last year it happened again — stocks dropped 19% in April and closed the year up 16%.

Why? Markets price fear instantly, but the recovery doesn’t send a notification. The drop is loud. The finish is silent. People remember the crash and miss the year. And selling at the bottom converts a normal 14% dip into a permanent loss — the yearly drop doesn’t cost most people money, their reaction to it does.

Honest caveat: 11 of those 46 years did finish down. The pattern is strong. It is not a promise.

The market charges a toll every year: about 14% of fear. Pay it, and you usually get the finish. Panic, and you only get the crash.

A dying video game store took down one of Wall Street’s biggest hedge funds. Then someone turned off the buy button.

In 2020, GameStop was a mall store selling discs in a download world, so hedge funds bet on its death. They borrowed shares, sold them, and planned to buy them back cheaper. That’s a short. And they shorted so much that 140% of the available shares had been sold short, more than actually existed, because borrowed shares were re-lent and shorted again.

Reddit spotted the flaw. If enough people bought and refused to sell, the shorts would eventually have to buy those shares back from the only people holding them. The price rose, the shorts had to buy to stop their losses, and their buying pushed it higher still. $17.25 became $483 in three weeks. One major fund lost 53% in a single month and needed a $2.75 billion rescue.

Then at the peak, major brokers restricted buying while selling stayed on, and the price collapsed within hours. Traders called it rigged. The brokers said their clearinghouses demanded billions in collateral overnight. Congress held hearings. Both explanations still have believers.

The real lesson: Wall Street didn’t lose because it was wrong about GameStop. It lost because everyone was wrong together, in the same direction. Crowded trades don’t fail quietly. They explode.

Was turning off that button protection, or protection for the wrong side?

The smartest man who ever lived lost a fortune in the stock market. He discovered gravity. He couldn’t resist a bubble.

In 1720, Isaac Newton had explained gravity, invented calculus, and was running England’s money as Master of the Royal Mint. That same year, England went insane over one stock: the South Sea Company. The price rose 700% in months. Servants were buying. Poets were buying. Parliament was buying.

Newton was in early, and when the mania started he did the smart thing. He sold, doubled his money, and walked away. He reportedly said he could calculate the motions of the heavens, but not the madness of the people.

Then the price kept rising without him. His friends kept getting richer. And the smartest man alive cracked. He bought back in at triple his original price, near the very top, even converting his safe government bonds to buy more. Months later the stock collapsed from over £1,000 back to where it started. He lost around £20,000, millions in today’s money, and for the rest of his life he forbade anyone to say the words “South Sea” in his presence.

His mistake wasn’t stupidity. He’d already made the smart move once. His mistake was watching other people get rich. Intelligence can price a company. It cannot price your envy.

The most expensive sentence in investing is “everyone else is making money.”

A janitor died with $8 million. That same year, a Wall Street executive went bankrupt. Neither was an accident.

One of them understood markets better than almost anyone alive. The other never took a finance class. The janitor won, because investing isn’t a test of intelligence, it’s a test of patience. Read had time and no debt. Fuscone had debt and no time.

The stock market says Apple is worth $4.6 trillion. Nobody has ever paid that, and nobody could.

Market cap sounds like a price tag, but it’s just multiplication: the last price one share traded at, multiplied by all 14.6 billion shares that exist. And on a normal day, less than 1% of those shares actually trade. So a small group of buyers sets today’s price, and that price gets applied to every share in existence. Almost all of Apple’s value was never bought by anyone. It was extrapolated.

Which is why “a trillion dollars was wiped off the market” is a strange sentence. No money was destroyed and nothing was withdrawn. The last trade simply happened at a lower number, and everyone re-multiplied.

It’s also why the richest people aren’t liquid. Their fortunes aren’t in bank accounts, they’re multiplications, which is why they borrow against shares instead of selling them.

Market cap isn’t money that exists. It’s an estimate built from the smallest trades of the day, and it’s completely real right up until everyone tries to collect it.

Is market cap a real number, or a very confident guess?

Nearly $1 trillion in gold sits 80 feet under Manhattan — and almost none of it belongs to America. 

The vault beneath the New York Fed holds roughly 6,000 tons, resting on bedrock because nothing else could take the weight. The US owns about 5% of it. The US economy grew 1.5 points last quarter. AI infrastructure spending — led by Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta — contributed about 1.15 of them. 

Those four spent $165 billion on chips and data centers in a single quarter, up 87% in a year, with ~$725 billion planned for 2026. AI construction is now roughly 5% of GDP — a level last seen in the late-90s tech boom. Strip that spending out, and the headline growth almost disappears.

The S&P 500 just hit record highs — and its forward P/E fell below where it started the year. 

That shouldn’t be possible. But a P/E ratio is just a fraction: price divided by earnings. Everyone watches the price. Almost nobody watches the earnings — and right now, earnings are booming. Over 20% growth two quarters straight, tracking 23%+ this quarter versus a 16% five-year average. When the “E” grows faster than the “P,” the market climbs and gets cheaper at the same time.

One honest catch: cheaper than January doesn’t mean cheap — 20x earnings is still above the ten-year average, and forward earnings are only estimates.

So — healthiest bull market in years, or borrowed time before earnings catch down?

The S&P 500 since 1993: about +27% during trading hours. Over +1,000% while the market was closed. 📊

Nearly all of the market’s gains arrive overnight — in the gap between yesterday’s close and today’s open. Earnings drop after the bell, big news lands before it, and holding through the night is a risk the market pays you for.

But before you build a strategy on it: two trades a day means spreads, costs, and taxes eat the entire edge. The anomaly is real — the free lunch isn’t.

The market doesn’t pay you for watching. It pays you for staying.

The Strategy Behind an 11,376% Trading Return

Most retail traders see an aggressive gap down and immediately rush to short the market. Legendary trader Larry Williams did the exact opposite.  
Using setups like this, Williams generated an 11,376% return to win the 1987 World Cup Trading Championship. Here is how his famous OOPS Strategy works when a morning move fails:  
1. The Setup (Gap Down)
Price opens significantly below the previous day’s low. Retail sentiment turns heavily bearish, but opening weakness alone is not an entry signal.  
2. The Trap (Wait for Failure)
Instead of chasing the gap down, sit on your hands and wait. Watch whether sellers have real follow-through or if the opening sell-off starts stalling.  
3. The Trigger (The Reclaim)
Wait for price to reverse and climb back toward the previous session’s range. The instant price crosses back above yesterday’s low, the trap is sprung and the long entry triggers.  
4. Risk Management
 Stop Loss: Below the newly formed morning swing low.  
 Take Profit Target: Aim toward the prior day’s high.  
Note: Stop and target levels are illustrative examples, not rigid rules. Larry used additional market filters alongside this core pattern.

During the 2008 financial crisis, many investors found themselves trapped in exactly that situation—selling meant locking in substantial losses, while staying invested meant remaining exposed to further downside.
 
That’s where hedging can become important.
 
For investors with large holdings, a hedge can help reduce market exposure and potentially soften the impact of major downturns without necessarily liquidating the entire position.
 
The goal isn’t to predict every crash. It’s to understand how much risk you’re carrying before one arrives.

In this reel, a trading psychologist shares a powerful lesson inspired by addiction recovery. People committed to overcoming alcohol abuse are often encouraged to attend **90 meetings in 90 days**. The goal isn’t just to gain knowledge—it’s to repeat the right behavior until it becomes part of who they are.
 
The same principle applies to trading. Instead of trying to change ten habits at once, pick **one**. Maybe it’s following your stop loss without exception. Maybe it’s sizing every position correctly. Maybe it’s letting your winners run. Then commit to practicing that one behavior every single day for the next 90 days.
 
Real transformation doesn’t happen because you understand a concept. It happens because you repeat it long enough that it becomes automatic. That’s how discipline is built, and that’s how lasting trading habits are formed.
 
Because successful traders don’t change overnight—they change one habit at a time, until excellence becomes second nature.

In this reel, a trading psychologist explains why many traders make the mistake of documenting only their losses, mistakes, and negative emotions. While it’s important to learn from failures, constantly replaying what went wrong can train your mind to focus on weakness instead of excellence.
 
The best traders and hedge fund managers take a different approach. They carefully study and journal their **best trades**. They revisit the moments when they followed their plan, managed risk perfectly, stayed disciplined, and executed with confidence. By repeatedly reinforcing successful behaviors, they teach their brains exactly what winning looks like.
 
Think of it like raising a child. If all you ever point out are mistakes, confidence slowly disappears. But if you consistently reinforce good habits and positive behaviors, those actions become second nature.
 
Because the fastest way to improve isn’t just by fixing your weaknesses—it’s by repeating your strengths until they become automatic.

What do surgeons and successful traders have in common? More than you might think.
 
In this reel, a trading psychologist draws a fascinating comparison between medical training and trading. When surgeons are learning, they don’t let emotions take over after one successful operation or one mistake. They don’t suffer from FOMO, chase more surgeries, or abandon their process. Instead, they stay grounded, receive constant feedback, review their performance, and gradually improve through deliberate practice.
 
Trading should be no different. Yet many traders let emotions dictate their next decision. After a loss, they revenge trade. After missing a move, they chase the market. Instead of learning from every trade, they react emotionally and repeat the same mistakes.
 
The traders who improve the fastest are the ones who treat every trade as feedback—not as a verdict on their abilities. They review, adapt, and keep refining their process until disciplined execution becomes second nature.
 
Because mastery isn’t built by chasing the next trade. It’s built through consistent feedback, continuous learning, and staying grounded under pressure.

**Your Strategy Can’t Save You From This**
 
Many traders believe that once they have a systematic trading strategy, emotions no longer matter. But that’s one of the biggest misconceptions in trading. No matter how mechanical your system is, **you’re still the one making the decisions.**
 
In this reel, a trader explains why your mental state has a direct impact on your performance. If you’re dealing with stress, personal problems, anxiety, or emotional exhaustion, those feelings can quietly influence your judgment. **Trading Is a Game of Regret**
 

One of the hardest truths about trading is that you’ll almost never feel completely satisfied with a trade. Exit too early, and you’ll regret the profits you could have made. Exit too late, and you’ll regret not taking money off the table. No matter what you do, the market always gives you a reason to think, **”What if?”**
 
In this reel, a seasoned trader explains why regret is an unavoidable part of the trading journey. The key isn’t trying to eliminate it—it’s learning to make decisions based on discipline, probability, and your trading plan instead of hindsight. Every trade should be judged by the quality of your execution, not by how far the market moved after you exited.
 
The best traders understand that no one consistently captures the exact top or bottom of every move. Their edge comes from executing their strategy repeatedly, accepting that they’ll leave money on the table, and refusing to let regret influence their next decision.
 
Because in trading, chasing the perfect exit is a losing game. Consistently following your process is what builds long-term success.

Spreads matter. A lot.

A strategy can look profitable on paper and still lose money live simply because the edge is smaller than the cost of executing it.

Imagine your average trade only has a tiny statistical advantage.

Now subtract the spread from every single entry and exit.

Once? Barely noticeable.

Over 100, 500 or 1,000 trades?

It can completely change the equity curve.

And the more frequently your strategy trades — especially on lower timeframes with tight targets — the more important this becomes.

That’s why a strategy isn’t finished when the backtest looks good.

You need to ask:

Does the edge still exist after realistic trading costs?

Because you don’t trade the backtest.

You trade what’s left after execution.

The pattern is uncomfortably familiar 📈

2000: Fed hiked into the dot-com bubble. Market fell 50%. 
2008: rates rose into a housing crisis. System nearly collapsed. 
2022: aggressive hikes triggered a 30% correction. 

Every single time, the story was the same. Higher rates make borrowing expensive. Markets re-price lower.

Now oil is up 70% since the start of the year. Americans are paying close to $4 a gallon again. Wheat is up 30%. The Bloomberg Commodity Index is back at 2022 peak levels. If these moves feed through to consumer prices, inflation could push back toward 3 to 4%, the level that has historically forced the Fed to act.

But here's the critical distinction. This inflation is being driven by supply disruption, not a fundamental surge in demand. Historically that makes it more short-lived. Once tensions ease or supply adjusts, prices tend to normalise.

The question is whether the Fed waits to find out or acts before it has the answer.

Gold is doing something it has only done twice in recorded history 🪙

Its market value now equals 170% of the entire US money supply. The only two times we've seen this before were 1933: when banks failed, unemployment hit 25%, and the dollar was devalued by 40% overnight and 1980, when inflation hit 14% and gold surged 20x before crashing 60% once the crisis passed.

Here's what makes today different. The economy still looks healthy. Inflation is nowhere near 1970s levels. There are no mass bank failures. And yet gold is acting as if something beneath the surface is starting to crack.

Is gold the smartest asset in the room right now or is it getting ahead of itself?

Link in bio | Larry Fink asked the SEC for one thing in January 2025. On September 17, 2026, he got it.

The order is called the Innovation Exemption. For five years, until September 2031, tokenized US stocks can legally trade onchain inside America, and the venues running that trading don’t need an exchange licence. Two conditions matter. The token has to be a real share, with the same dividends and the same votes as the original, so the synthetic versions sold offshore don’t qualify. The last time the SEC used this tool for something this new was 1992, for a product Wall Street called a gimmick. ETFs grew for 26 years on more than 300 of those exemptive orders before they got a rule of their own. Today they hold over ten trillion dollars.

The wildest part is the name. Cede & Co. is not a person or a family. It stands for “Central Depository.”

Here is where it came from. In 1968, Wall Street was so buried in paper stock certificates that the New York Stock Exchange shut down every Wednesday for half the year just to catch up. Brokers were going under from the backlog. The fix, in 1973, was to stop moving the paper at all. Lock every certificate in one vault, register it all under one nominee name, and track who really owns what in a database. That nominee was Cede & Co. It made stocks digital, sort of. The paper never left the vault. You just stopped seeing it.

That patch is now fifty years old, and it is finally being replaced. A token does the same job the 1973 vault did, except the asset itself becomes the record. Nothing to immobilize, nothing to reconcile overnight, nothing held under someone else’s name.

The last time the system was rebuilt this way, it created Visa and Mastercard. This time, a new company is taking over the process.

The Fed doesn’t “print money.” What they actually do is far more interesting, and far more consequential for your wealth.

In 1907, America had no central bank. When banks started failing, one man: JP Morgan, had to personally bail out the financial system. The government realized they needed a mechanism to prevent this from happening again. In 1913, the Federal Reserve was created.

For decades, the Fed did one simple thing: set interest rates. Raise rates to cool the economy. Lower rates to heat it up. Everyone understood it.

Then 2008 broke everything.

The Fed invented “Quantitative Easing” (QE). Here’s what that actually means: The Fed creates digital money and uses it to buy bonds from banks. Banks now have cash instead of bonds. That cash flows into stocks, real estate, and risk assets. Prices rise.

But only for people who already owned assets.

If you had a stock portfolio in 2009, you watched it multiply. If you didn’t, you watched housing become unaffordable and your savings lose purchasing power. This is why insiders call the Fed “the engine of inequality.”

Today’s Fed is a three-headed beast: rate policy, balance sheet (QE), and bank regulation. These three heads interact in ways that even the people running the system don’t fully understand.
The Fed currently loses about $100 billion per year. They bought bonds when prices were high (rates were low). Now they’re underwater. That loss adds to the deficit. Which requires more debt. Which eventually requires more money creation.

This cycle is why hard assets (gold, real estate, Bitcoin) keep climbing while savings accounts earn nothing.

The system isn’t broken. It’s working exactly as designed. The question is: which side of it are you on?

A possible risk to markets you need to know, from Tokyo not Washington.

For decades, Japan kept rates at or near zero and turned the yen into the world’s favourite funding currency. Funds could borrow cheaply in yen, flip it into dollars, and lever up into higher-return assets: U.S. growth stocks, bonds, even crypto. The yen carry trade didn’t create this bull market, but it definitely poured gasoline on it.

Now that regime is shifting. The Bank of Japan has already lifted rates off zero and allowed long-term yields to break out to levels we haven’t seen in roughly 17 years. When Japanese rates rise and the yen strengthens, that “free” funding stops being free. Risk managers don’t argue with that math, they slash exposure, starting with the most crowded trades.

August 2024 was an example: a BoJ shift, a yen spike, Japanese stocks nuked double digits in a day, U.S. tech and Bitcoin puked… and then most of it was retraced once the forced selling cleared.

That’s the pattern to internalise. BoJ tightening doesn’t automatically kill AI or crypto, it changes how violently we correct when leverage gets squeezed.

Watch BoJ meetings, Japanese bond yields, and sudden yen strength as your early warning system. When those line up and markets air-pocket 15–20%, it usually feels like the end of the world. Historically, it’s where the best entries show up.

One new law is gonna cause a lot of crypto to crash. BUT, that same law will also cause a few to fly.

For years crypto’s had one big problem: unclear regulations. This causes two things: First, big money stayed away from crypto to avoid getting into accidental trouble and second, the good founders don’t know how to comply so many of them avoided launching a token.

The SEC used to say most tokens are securities, because a test from 1946 said so. Imagine the mess we were in. They’ve hit projects with lawsuits but refused to write new rules.

That’s left the market in a mess: banks are hesitant, innovators are heading overseas, and honest players have to guess what’s legal.

The CLARITY Act splits crypto into three buckets: securities, commodities, and stablecoins.

Every token wants to be a commodity because it means easier rules and large investor access. To qualify, the founding team needs to have less than 20% of the supply, voting power and they need to be open-source. In simple terms: if insiders control more than ~20% or can change the rules on their own, regulators treat it as “controlled,” not truly decentralized. 

Those “controlled” tokens get pushed into the securities lane: stricter disclosures, lockups, and real limits on where and how they can trade. A lot of the casino-style coins with huge insider allocations are going to get squeezed or delisted in the U.S.

Meanwhile, the assets that are decentralized, useful, open-source and widely held become digital commodities under the CFTC. That’s the lane where banks, ETFs, and serious funds can finally get full, clean exposure with clear rules instead of guessing. 

Stablecoins get their own rulebook: 1:1 high-quality reserves, tight licensing, no “stake your stablecoin for yield,” and coin holders sit at the front of the line in a bankruptcy. 

So what happens when this kicks in? The junk with bad structures and insider control bleeds. The few networks that actually meet the bar for decentralization and transparency become the only game in town for big, regulated money and that’s where the real upside will be.

Financial nihilism isn’t just “people got more degenerate.” It’s what happens when the maths of life stop making sense.

You grow up hearing “work hard, save, buy a home”… then realise: Housing went 10x, salaries didn’t and cash in the bank bleeds to inflation, your brain does the only logical thing in an illogical system: “If long-term doesn’t work for me, I might as well gamble now.”

That’s financial nihilism, the belief that the future is so rigged, the only rational move is to swing for impossible odds today.

But that belief is exactly what turns you from investor into exit liquidity. Because while you’re chasing the next 1,000x meme, real protocols with real cash flow are compounding quietly in the background.

Save this as a reminder: the system wants you impatient. Your edge is refusing to play the clown in someone else’s casino.

And, Microstrategy has been a dead stock since the dotcom bubble, this shift brought it back to life and into new highs.

But once crypto became legal and ETFs were created, the continued presence of these stocks made no sense. A company holding Bitcoin on their balance sheet as a hedge against inflation or for diversification is fine and actually smart, but a company whose stock becomes a pure proxy for a digital asset is nothing more than a middleman on leverage.

The hype makes them trade at a premium to the underlying digital asset (DA) and they even perform better than the coin they hold because of that hype. This helped these same companies go out and raise more debt, to buy coins, boosting DA and stock prices higher, to re-raise debt, etc. An endless loophole?

• True Ownership: Cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum are decentralized, meaning no single entity controls them. You hold the keys to your wealth.

• Beating the System: By embracing decentralized finance (DeFi), you’re opting out of a system that benefits the few and joining a movement that empowers the many.

The choice is between a future where you’re monitored and controlled, or one where you’re free to manage your own wealth.

Since 1 July, most cheap parcels ordered online from outside the EU pay at least €3 in customs duty: €3 per kind of item, on parcels up to €150. By law a business normally owes the charge, not the buyer. Temu and AliExpress add it at checkout, and Shein says its prices include it.

Each of these parcels gets its own customs form. In Belgium, which receives more of them than any other EU country, customs counted 53% fewer forms in July than a year earlier. Dutch customs handled about 22 million in June and 7.7 million in the first 25 days of August.

Fewer forms do not have to mean fewer purchases. France charged €2 per item from March to June, and its customs forms fell from about 500,000 a day to 50,000. On 13 May the head of French customs told parliament the parcels had mostly been redirected to neighbouring countries. He had no figure for how many fewer reached French homes. He also predicted the next move, perfectly legal in his words: ship in bulk, store the goods in Europe, deliver from there. Bulk goods are cleared under normal import rules before sale, and deliveries inside Europe then need no import form. On 1 September, Dutch customs said more and more companies seem to be doing that.

Poland’s finance ministry says prices rose by the amount of the charge and that this is the main reason imports fell. Shein’s first report as a listed company, out on 28 September, says it sold less in Europe from April to June, before the charge, as it raised prices and cut online advertising. It names more stock inside Europe as a priority. A second EU charge of €2 per kind of item is expected in November. The published figures do not yet show how much of the drop is fewer purchases and how much is goods arriving another way.

Sources: Reg. (EU) 2026/382; European Commission; FOD Financiën; Douane Nederland; Assemblée nationale; Polish finance ministry; Shein; Reuters.

On 26 September, a passenger’s power bank caught fire near a seat on Lufthansa flight LH1170 from Frankfurt to Lisbon. The crew sealed it in a fireproof bag, the pilots declared an emergency and the A321 landed in Lyon. Nobody was hurt, Lufthansa said.

Power banks are banned from checked bags and must travel with the passenger. The reason is how they burn. In FAA tests, heating a lithium cell to 204–232 °C set off thermal runaway: the cell heats itself, its case can pass 760 °C and it can set off the cell next to it. A gas extinguisher can knock the flames down but does not stop that chain. The FAA’s guidance is to cool the battery with large amounts of water, which only someone in the cabin can pour. In the hold nobody can, and in FAA tests the cargo-hold Halon did not stop the spread from cell to cell.

On 28 January 2025, an Air Busan A321 burned out on the ground in Busan before take-off. All 176 people on board got out. In March, Korean investigators said the likely cause was a power bank in an overhead bin. Since then the rules have moved power banks closer to the passenger. EASA and the FAA want them kept in sight and within reach, and since 15 January 2026 the Lufthansa Group has banned them from overhead bins.

The FAA verified 97 lithium battery incidents on planes and in air cargo in 2025, about twice the 47 of 2017, and says its list is not complete. In the EU, an event like the LH1170 fire must be reported under Regulation 2015/1018, and EASA says such reports are rising. It does not publish how many. Germany’s aviation authority publishes yearly counts of laser attacks on planes, 365 in 2025, with no line for batteries.

Sources: Lufthansa via dpa and RTL; adsb.lol; FAA (TC-16/37, SAFO 25002, SAFO 15010, InFO 17008, incident dashboard); ARAIB; EASA SIB 2025-03; Reg. (EU) 2015/1018; Lufthansa Group; LBA.

On 25 September, President Lula signed a provisional decree banning licensed online sports betting and casino-style games. New deposits stopped that day. People can withdraw through the apps until 23:59 Brasília time on 5 October; the licensed sites are due to close on 6 October, and banks are due to refund remaining balances between 9 and 14 October.

In 2025, bettors deposited about R$230 billion with licensed betting companies (over 40 billion dollars) and lost about R$41 billion: the companies’ gaming revenue before taxes and costs. These are SIGAP figures, extracted 8 September and published by iGaming Brazil; the regulator’s January report said R$37 billion; the gap is unexplained. Withdrawals are not in the published figures.

The government presents the ban as protection for families in debt. In August 2024, Brazil’s central bank estimated that 5 million people in Bolsa Família families sent R$3 billion to betting companies: gross transfers, not a measure of benefit money lost. The Supreme Court then ordered benefit money kept out of betting.

Federal licensing began in January 2025, at R$30 million per licence. The decree ends the licences after 30 days with no refund, and the industry association ANJL says it will go to court. The industry argues people will keep betting on illegal sites; a study it paid for, modelled on a survey of bettors, estimates they already take about 41% of the money bet. It also bars payment firms from processing bets; whether that works is not yet known.

The decree came nine days before the 4 October election. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula’s main rival, called it populist, hypocritical and electioneering. In an AtlasIntel poll days earlier, 75% backed a ban. Congress must approve the decree in time, or it lapses.

Sources: MP 1.394; Ministry of Justice; SIGAP/iGaming Brazil; SPA; BCB; STF; LCA/IBJR; AtlasIntel; Estadão.

On 23 September, advisers to the US FDA voted 7 to 2, with one abstention, that the benefits of GRAIL’s Galleri blood test outweigh its risks. The day before, the NEJM published the largest randomised trial so far of a multi-cancer blood test, run with an earlier version of GRAIL’s test. Those tested did not end up with fewer stage 3 and 4 cancers than those whose blood went into a freezer.

In England, the NHS-Galleri trial randomised 142,250 people invited at ages 50 to 77 not under investigation for suspected cancer. One group’s blood was tested at up to three yearly visits, the other’s stored untested. In the first year the test flagged 419 cancers. Another 708 people were diagnosed with cancer within a year of a negative test, and nobody can say how many of those were already there.

Its main goal, fewer stage 3 and 4 cancers across 12 deadly types, was not met. The tested group’s rate was 1.03 times the frozen group’s, and none of the yearly differences could be told apart from chance. A planned secondary result showed 14% fewer stage 4 cancers, at the edge of chance, but more stage 3 cancers. GRAIL says some were caught before reaching stage 4. Richard Houlston of the Institute of Cancer Research, who declared no conflicts, called that explanation entirely speculative. The trial was funded by GRAIL.

The panel also voted 6 to 4 that the newer version of the test is effective and 10 to 0 that it is safe. GRAIL’s proposed use makes no claim of fewer stage 4 cancers, and the FDA did not ask the panel about that. Some panellists doubted it detects cancer early. The FDA has not decided yet. Cancer deaths in each group have not been published, and the trial’s designers wrote that it would be too small to compare them directly.

Sources: NEJM and Nature Medicine, 22.09.2026; ASCO 2026; Cancers 2022; FDA; STAT; AP; GenomeWeb; Science Media Centre; NPR.

On 21 September, France’s economy minister Roland Lescure said 17% of the country’s fuel stations were missing at least one fuel that morning, and that 91% of them were TotalEnergies stations: “a direct consequence of the price cap.”

TotalEnergies caps diesel at €2.25 and petrol at €1.99 at every station it runs in mainland France. On 20 September, 17 of 5,668 other stations with a fresh diesel price were at or below €2.25. Their median was €2.44.

In the government’s own shortage data, checked every day at noon since 1 January, a station counts as out when it has no diesel, or no petrol of any grade. Identified TotalEnergies stations are about 23% of the stations in that data. In January and February, before the cap, they were 34% of the stations that ran out. From 8 April to 30 June, with diesel capped at €2.25 everywhere, 80%. From 1 to 21 July, when Total narrowed the cap to about 1,200 rural stations and motorways on holiday weekends, 70%. Since it came back everywhere on 22 July, 86%. On 22 September, 46% of identified Total stations reported being out, against 2% of the others.

This is a pattern, not proof. Prices and holidays moved too. Shortages are self-declared, and the brand list may miss some stations in Total’s network.

TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanné says the cap raised its market share from 22% to 25%. In August he estimated its cost at €250 to 300 million. He has promised to keep it as long as the conflict lasts, and warned that there would never be another price cap if extra profits are taxed. Independent stations have filed an unfair-competition complaint with France’s competition authority; no published decision had been found by 23 September. On 23 September the government said France is not blocking an EU push for such a tax. No end date for the cap has been announced.

Sources: prix-carburants.gouv.fr open data; TotalEnergies releases; franceinfo; AFP; BFM; Le Figaro; Capital.

On 21 September, Amnesty International published a briefing on the Rubaya coltan mine in eastern Congo, held by the armed group M23 since April 2024: eighteen miners killed at Rubaya and at a gold mine in South Kivu, men kept digging underground for over a week. Neither M23 nor Rwandan officials responded to Amnesty.

A phone holds about forty milligrams of tantalum, dug up as the black ore called coltan. Witnesses told UN investigators of four or five trucks leaving Rubaya twice a week, up to five tonnes each. The UN put the flow at 120 to at least 150 tonnes a month, driven into Rwanda.

Rwanda’s central bank publishes coltan exports: about 1,000 tonnes in 2021, 2,743 in 2025, and 614 in July 2026 alone, the largest month in its series. UN experts wrote that the 2025 rise is not supported by Rwanda’s own production. In the months the witnesses described, Rwanda shipped about 195 tonnes a month; the convoys would account for 120, or at least 150.

Rwanda says it has its own reserves and a regulated, formalised mining sector, and told the UN it digs 8,000 to 9,000 tonnes a year of tin, tantalum and tungsten ore together. The UN wrote that Rwanda’s own statistics office contradicts that. The US Geological Survey’s production figure for Rwanda carries a footnote: reported exports.

Traxys, a Luxembourg trader, bought 280 tonnes from Rwanda in 2024, Global Witness found; it says none came from Rubaya. In June, Global Witness said five of Rwanda’s seven biggest exporters buy smuggled ore and sell to smelters in China and Kazakhstan, from where it likely reaches products from Sony, Microsoft and Amazon. Amazon says it asked suppliers for more due diligence; the ITSCI traceability scheme disputes the report. In April the UN asked Rwanda where the extra tonnes came from. By May, no answer.

Sources: Amnesty AFR 62/1454/2026; UN Group of Experts S/2024/969, S/2025/446, S/2026/466; National Bank of Rwanda; USGS; Global Witness; ITSCI.

On Friday the president of the United States posted that CNN, Politico and MS NOW were banned from the White House. On Saturday morning their reporters were stopped at the gate and their press passes were confiscated.

The room he banned them from has forty-nine assigned seats. He does not assign them. The White House Correspondents’ Association has done that since the Reagan administration, when fixed chairs replaced the old lounge furniture.

Last year his office tried to take that chart over and hand the seats out by audience size. The reporters refused. That chart never came. It did not need to: in January 2025 the White House had already added a fiftieth seat at the front of the room, for podcasters and influencers, and it fills that one itself.

This February the reporters redrew the room on their own terms. 66 outlets, 49 chairs, 33 of them changed, seven newsrooms seated for the first time. Four British newsrooms had a chair in 2022. Six have one now. The front row did not move.

The fourth chair in that front row belongs to the Associated Press. In February 2025 the AP was barred from the Oval Office and Air Force One for refusing to stop writing Gulf of Mexico, and the White House was explicit that it would keep its press pass. A judge ordered the doors reopened. An appeals court put that on hold, two to one: the president’s own rooms are not public forums, so he may choose who comes in. The same two judges drew a line. The briefing room is opened to the press generally, and there he may not.

So the chairs were never his to take. Nobody took a chair. They took the passes.

Sources: WHCA board letter 04.02.2026 and the 2022 and 2026 seating charts; WHCA statement 18.09.2026; Axios 30.03.2025; POLITICO 31.03.2025; AP v. Budowich, D.C. Cir. 25-5109; CBS News and NBC News, 19.09.2026.

On 15 September, Italian jets shot down a drone near Kaunas about twenty minutes after Lithuania’s armed forces observed it heading in around midnight. On 24 July, Romania’s radar picked up a drone off the Danube delta at 09:39 and a Romanian F-16 fired at 11:02: eighty-three minutes on the radar, by our count, over an unpopulated area near Padina.

Among the incidents shown here, the time from the first moment an army published to the moment a jet fired runs from about a quarter of an hour to eighty-three minutes. That first moment differs: a radar contact in Romania, a public alert in Estonia and Latvia, an observation in Lithuania.

Estonia in May: about a quarter of an hour from the alert to the shot. Latvia in June: 47 minutes from the first warning, as reported by LRT and LETA. Finland in August: a crewed Russian reconnaissance aircraft is suspected of about three minutes inside, and no shot has been reported.

The phones run a second clock. In Galati on 16 August the drone was shot at 05:01 and the RO-Alert reached phones at 05:08. It was already on the ground.

Where a government has explained the wait, it named the ground. Romania’s ministry says its pilot fired over an unpopulated area. When a balloon spent a week over North America in 2023, the President authorised the shot as soon as it could be done without undue risk to the people under its path. That took three more days, until it was over the sea.

Estonia’s drone was likely of Ukrainian origin, its military says, and it flew in under heavy Russian electronic warfare. Latvia’s was Ukrainian, its armed forces say, most likely pushed in by Russian electronic warfare. Where Lithuania’s was launched from, no government has said.

Sources: Lithuanian Armed Forces; NKVC via LRT and BNS; MApN via Agerpres and Viata Libera; mil.ee via ERR; Latvian NBS, LRT, LETA; Finnish Border Guard; US Department of Defense, 4 February 2023.

On Monday in Cardiff the leaders of Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn Féin signed a memorandum saying each of their nations has the right to decide its own future, and calling on the British government to “prepare for, plan and facilitate constitutional change”. They signed as party leaders, not as governments.

The film draws one line and asks who gets to draw it. In 2016, 51.9 of every 100 votes inside Great Britain said leave the European Union. Count the same ballots inside smaller lines and the verdicts change: Scotland 38.0, Northern Ireland 44.2, Wales 52.5, England 53.4.

Scotland drew its own line once. In 2014, 44.7 of 100 said yes to independence, on a vote two governments had signed for in Edinburgh. In 2022 the UK Supreme Court ruled unanimously that the Scottish Parliament cannot hold that vote alone.

What would a vote say now? Nobody knows; these are polls, not counts. With undecided removed: Scotland 52 yes (Survation, August), Wales 32 (Survation, same weeks), Northern Ireland 42 for a united Ireland (Institute of Irish Studies and Sunday Times, May).

Andy Burnham told John Swinney a referendum was off limits in July and repeated it in writing on 10 September. On Saturday in Dublin Donald Trump said he would love to see a united Ireland and “it may as well happen now”. Downing Street answered the same day: the support the Good Friday Agreement requires is not there.

That agreement holds the only written rule: London must call a border poll when it appears likely a majority would vote for a united Ireland. It does not say what likely means. Scotland asked for the same rule and was told no. The Prime Minister is expected to meet all three next month.

Sources: House of Commons Library, UK Supreme Court (23.11.2022), Northern Ireland Act 1998, Survation tables, Institute of Irish Studies, Sinn Féin, gov.scot, BBC, Guardian, RTÉ.

On 12 September, ten governments adopted the New Delhi Declaration at the BRICS summit in India. It runs to 140 paragraphs. The word Ukraine is not in it.

The four previous declarations all had it. Beijing 2022 mentioned Ukraine three times and backed talks between Russia and Ukraine. Johannesburg 2023, Kazan 2024 and Rio 2025 each recalled the members’ “national positions” once. New Delhi 2026: none.

Iran is the second word. Last year’s paper condemned “the military strikes against the Islamic Republic of Iran”. This year’s condemns attacks on nuclear facilities under IAEA safeguards and names no state. Tariffs are condemned without naming who set them.

The table has grown. Four founders in 2009, South Africa in 2010, then Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the Emirates in 2024 and Indonesia in 2025. The host counts Saudi Arabia as an eleventh member. Riyadh says its foreign minister came as an invited country. Around the table sit Russia, at war in Ukraine since 2022, and Iran beside the Emirates it has fired missiles at this year. Twice in 2026 the bloc’s foreign ministers met in Delhi and left without a joint statement. The chair’s note says “differing views”.

On the sidelines, Iran’s president met Abu Dhabi’s crown prince. The Emirati readout speaks of easing tensions. Washington has answered BRICS before, with a threat of 100% tariffs in 2024 and “a little group called BRICS, and it is fading out fast” in 2025. To this declaration, by Sunday afternoon, there was no statement from the White House, the State Department, the European Commission or the EEAS.

Paragraph 140 hands the 2027 chair to China.

The film counts the word across the five texts, page by page.

Sources: PM India and MEA (New Delhi Declaration and special briefing, 12 September 2026), BRICS 2026 archive (2022 to 2025 texts), Kremlin, Saudi Press Agency, Abu Dhabi Media Office, Truth Social archive, White House.

On 11 September, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said the East-West Pipeline had been shut as a precaution, a day after drones hit it in the Riyadh and Madinah regions. The kingdom says the drones came from Iraq. Iraq confirmed the launch site in Maysan and dismissed a commander. Iran-aligned militias denied any role. No group has claimed responsibility.

The pipeline matters because it is the way round the Strait of Hormuz: 1,200 km to Yanbu on the Red Sea, where Saudi crude has been leaving since the strait closed in March. From Yanbu the oil goes south through Bab el-Mandeb to Asia, or north through Egypt to Europe.

The south route has been under a Houthi blockade on Saudi shipping since 20 July. On 11 September the Houthis took Perim island, in the middle of Bab el-Mandeb, and their spokesman said the sea is safe for everyone except Saudi ships. Saudi exports to Asia fell from 3.4 million barrels a day in June to 128,000 in August, by Kpler’s count.

In the Gulf, Aramco began loading again in August. On 31 August two tankers carrying Saudi crude were hit as they left Hormuz. Two sailors died. Riyadh blamed Iran.

Kpler estimates Saudi crude exports at 3.2 million barrels a day in August, the lowest in 13 years. The ministry says further developments will be announced in due course. Its statement gives no date for the pipeline.

The film counts the three ways out on a relief map, with the shipping lanes drawn from OpenStreetMap traffic-separation schemes and the SUMED pipeline across Egypt. Where a lane is sketched rather than mapped, the ground says so.

Sources: Saudi Press Agency, Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs via Al Jazeera, Reuters, AP, Kpler via Al-Monitor and CNBC.

On 10 September, in Venice, a documentary called NAZA put 24 anonymised Israeli intelligence and military officers on screen. The title is an army term for the civilians a strike is expected to kill. Before a home in Gaza is bombed, that number is written down.

In April 2024, officers told +972 Magazine, Local Call and the Guardian that in the first weeks of the war they were permitted 15 or 20 civilians for one junior Hamas operative, and on several occasions more than 100 for a commander. One said he spent about 20 seconds on a target before approving it. In the film, one officer says the number once reached 500.

The homes were chosen on purpose. Officers said a target is easiest to find at night, when he is home with his family, and that cheap unguided bombs were used on junior names. Sometimes the house came down and the target was not inside.

In January 2025 the army’s chief of staff said 20,000 fighters had been killed. Four months later the army’s own database of dead fighters, held about 8,900 names. The Gaza health ministry’s count of the dead then stood at 53,000.

The Israeli military says it firmly rejects the film’s allegations, that anonymous witnesses cannot be verified, and that it makes unprecedented efforts to minimise harm to civilians. In its written answer of April 2024 it said every target gets an individual assessment of expected collateral damage, that such assessments are not made categorically, and that it does not strike when the expected damage is excessive in relation to the military advantage.

So a number exists for every strike. What it was, strike by strike, nobody has published.

The map is drawn from OpenStreetMap, copyright OpenStreetMap contributors.

Sources: the Guardian, 10 and 11 Sept 2026; Reuters, 10 Sept; IDF statement, 11 Sept; +972 Magazine and the Guardian, 3 April 2024; IDF written response, 3 April 2024; +972 Magazine, 21 Aug 2025.

On 9 September 2026, about an hour into his Dallas convention keynote, President Trump promised a $5,000 “dividend” to every adult US citizen if Republicans keep the House and the Senate on 3 November. The bill for that, on Time’s count of 240 million adult citizens, is $1.2 trillion (CRFB).

This film does not measure the size. It checks what arrived, promise by promise. February 2025: an adviser’s $5,000 per taxpaying household from “DOGE” savings; Trump called it a great idea; nothing was paid. November 2025: at least $2,000 a person from tariffs, in Trump’s own post; the same day his Treasury Secretary said it might just mean the tax cuts already passed; ten months on, no cheque. December 2025: $1,776 to 1.45 million service members, paid within days as a housing-allowance supplement. Trump said tariffs paid for it; officials said Congress had voted the money in July, for housing, and the Pentagon repurposed it. Also in law: $1,000 for every newborn. In January 2021 the other party made the same kind of promise before the Georgia runoff: $1,400 landed ten weeks later, on top of $600 Trump had signed eight days before Biden spoke, because Congress passed a bill.

For the $5,000 there is, as of 11 September, no bill and no mechanism. Trump told CBS News Texas he does not think Congress is needed and that “we’ve taken in trillions of dollars in tariffs.” Treasury’s July statement shows $154.5 billion of customs duties this fiscal year, net of $114.7 billion refunded after the Supreme Court struck down most of the tariffs in February. That is about one dollar in eight of the cost. The Senate majority leader is open to the idea; one senator says he will write a bill after the vote.

On 28 August 2026 Meta said its AI glasses would stop recording the moment the capture light is covered. Days later it confirmed it had disabled the cameras on glasses whose light had been tampered with: fewer than one pair in a thousand, of more than 7 million sold last year. The light is 2 millimetres wide.

Meta’s own bystander privacy paper says more. The camera does two jobs: saving photos and videos, and answering questions about what it sees. The light blinks only for the first. For AI features it stays off, because a light that blinked all the time would stop being noticed. So the light tells a bystander that a video is being saved, not that the camera is on.

On 9 September Apple announced the Watch Series 12 with two listening features. Live Rewind shows the last 15 seconds of a conversation as text after a double press, with a chime that plays even on silent. Siri Recap takes notes on whole conversations in the background. For those notes, Apple states there is no audible signal because no raw audio is retained. Neither feature is available in the EU at launch.

Norway’s government said on 25 August it may ban face recognition in glasses and set up an expert group without a deadline. Oslo banned smart glasses in every municipal school from 27 August. Its deputy mayor for education wrote that a school rule stops the glasses in the classroom, not on the metro and not outside the school gate.

Europe’s privacy regulators commissioned a report on whether people accept smart glasses, due in summer 2026. As of 11 September it has not been published.

The 3D watch shown is an earlier generation. Cover photo: ItzANormalFioko, CC BY-SA 3.0.

On 8 September 2026 OpenAI said an internal model had solved the Navier-Stokes problem, one of the seven million-dollar Millennium Prize Problems. OpenAI’s account: a rumour on 1 September, about a hundred AI agents on the simpler Euler equations, then some ten thousand on the prize problem, and a solution on 5 September, about 88 hours after the first agents started. The claim: a model of a fluid at rest whose core shrinks while its predicted speed grows without bound before a fixed time. No real fluid can do that, so the equations would fail. A computer has checked the proof. The Clay Mathematics Institute has not accepted it.

Hours earlier, Tristan Buckmaster of New York University and Levent Alpöge of Anthropic published a related breakdown for the frictionless equations, after a year of private work with AI tools, including OpenAI’s. Buckmaster’s account of two calls on 6 September: two proposals, one of which would have had him write up OpenAI’s result alone, without Alpöge. He refused both. OpenAI says it offered a joint release and to recognise their priority. Its researcher Sébastien Bubeck says he never asked for Alpöge’s removal from his own work. On 10 September Buckmaster called that account false. Both proofs build on the work of Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa.

One question stays open. Buckmaster asked whether the model had trained on the drafts the pair typed into OpenAI’s tools. OpenAI’s Mark Chen says no human or agent looked at user data for this. OpenAI’s post says it cannot rule out an indirect contribution through de-identified data. Whether their drafts helped is unknown.

The object in the film is an illustration, not a measurement. Alpöge works at Anthropic, whose Claude models helped make this film.

Sources: OpenAI post and paper, 8 Sept 2026; T. Buckmaster, statement, Euler paper and posts, 8 and 10 Sept 2026; Clay Mathematics Institute; S. Bubeck and M. Chen on X, 8 Sept 2026.

In 2013 a new German party, the AfD, got 4.7% of the vote and no seats. On 6 September 2026 it got 43.8% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, in eastern Germany. It was founded to end the euro. Thirteen years of one number: its share of the valid votes in every federal and state election it contested. Berlin 2021, annulled by the state’s constitutional court, is replaced by the 2023 repeat.

The party grew first in the five states that were East Germany until 1990. In 2015 its founder was voted out and about a fifth of the members left; that year over 400,000 people applied for asylum in Germany, and migration became the party’s main subject. It entered the Bundestag in 2017 with 12.6%, then fell, sharply in the West and less in the East. After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine it rose again: first place in Thuringia in 2024, 20.8% nationally in February 2025, and in March 2026 about double its last result in Baden-Württemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate.

Its basic programme, adopted in 2016, still demands an orderly end to the euro. Germany’s federal domestic intelligence agency has treated the party as a suspected extremist case since 2021, a classification two courts upheld. In May 2025 it upgraded the party to confirmed right-wing extremist; the party sued, and in February 2026 a Cologne court suspended the upgrade pending the main case. Four eastern state agencies keep their own classification. In Saxony-Anhalt the AfD holds 39 of 83 seats, three short of a majority, and so far no other party has agreed to govern with it. On 31 August, the US Federal Trade Commission and 22 states sued Amazon over the auction that prices the sponsored ads at the top of its search results. For years Amazon taught advertisers a simple rule: the winner pays one cent more than the next bid. Bid 75 cents, pay 61.

The complaint says that since July 2019, once each auction ends, Amazon has replaced its price for these ads with a higher one it sets itself, a “soft reserve” applied after the auction has run. It quotes the executive in charge of Amazon Ads: the second price “isn’t set by an actual bidder, but rather by a proxy 2nd price that we calculate.”

By the complaint’s numbers, the share of clicks charged at the winner’s full bid rose from 30-40% in 2021 to 70% in 2022 and close to 80% by 2024. During Prime Day 2023, it says, the hidden surcharges more than doubled the price of a click. Advertisers who asked were told it was higher shopper activity. The filing counts 1.2 million US advertisers and estimates the overcharge at more than 20 billion dollars. No court has ruled on it.

Amazon answered the same day. The lawsuit is “misguided”, it says, and the claim of company-wide deception “patently false”. The console where advertisers set bids has stated since 2018 that a bid is the maximum charge, and in 2024 some 92% of the ads it selected were not the highest bid.

Neither filing measures how much of this reached the prices shoppers paid. The FTC says a significant portion of sellers’ costs is passed through, and gives no number. Amazon notes the FTC’s own damages model assumes none was.

Sources: FTC et al. v. Amazon.com, Inc., Case 2:26-cv-03097, W.D. Wash., filed 31 August 2026; FTC press release, 31 August 2026; Amazon’s response, aboutamazon.com, 31 August 2026.

At 5:20 on Thursday morning the alarm went off at the museum in Villena, eastern Spain. Four minutes later, by the Spanish press’s reconstruction, the first patrol had the call. The thieves were already gone with most of the Treasure of Villena: bowls, bracelets and bottles, mostly gold, three thousand years old. As metal, the mayor puts it at up to 1.7 million euros. As history, archaeologists call it a unicum: one of a kind.

When the alarm works, why is the gold already gone? The Louvre’s timeline, from the Paris prosecutor, answers it. 9:34: two men walk into the Apollo Gallery and the alarm reaches the control room. 9:35: the manager phones the police station. 9:36: a team leader presses the button to police headquarters. 9:37: the message goes out to close every door. 9:38: they are out of the window. A phone call, a button, a message: four minutes, the same four the thieves needed.

In Alsace in July, the prosecutor timed the thieves on camera: eleven minutes inside the Musée Lalique. The alarm reached the monitoring company at once; the guards arrived ninety minutes later, the guard company confirms, and by then a cleaner had found the room and called the authorities.

Three days before Villena, Europol had described a pattern it saw across Europe: objects picked in advance, jobs planned, force brought along. Gold, because, in Europol’s words, “precious metals can be easily melted down, leaving no trace for law enforcement.”

As of 28 August, eight of the nine pieces taken from the Louvre were still missing, nobody had been arrested for Villena, and, as bowls and bracelets, nothing had come back.

On 26 August, the Frankfurt health office confirmed that two employees of Frankfurt airport had died of malaria this summer. Six caught it, at work, not on holiday. The first died in early July, and the malaria was found only after death.

Germany’s public health institute wrote down its assumption on 16 July: an infected mosquito, carried in on an aircraft. In 2021 and 2022, about sixty-six flights a day landed in the EU and EEA from countries where malaria is common. A 2024 European review counted the people who caught malaria without leaving: 145 cases since 1969, half of whom lived or worked at or near an airport. Frankfurt is eight of them. In none of those cases did a report find the infected mosquito. In 2022, Frankfurt set four traps, eighteen days after the likely bite. They caught one mosquito, the wrong kind, and it escaped. This summer’s catch is being examined in Antwerp.

The danger is the diagnosis. Nobody expects malaria in someone who never travelled, so it comes late: seven and a half days on average in the review’s cases. Seven in a hundred of those cases died. Among travellers, about one in a hundred. A late diagnosis, the institute writes, raises the risk of a severe course. In the review, every Frankfurt case survived. This summer, two did not. How long they waited is not published. A year earlier, two Frankfurt health-office authors had written in the region’s medical journal: ask a summer fever patient two more questions. Where do you work, and where do you live.

Whether anyone asked the six is not published. Whether those planes were sprayed, no one has said. The EU has no common rule.

Sources: RKI Epidemiologisches Bulletin 29/2026 (16 July 2026); dpa via DIE ZEIT and t-online, 26 August 2026; Hallmaier-Wacker et al., Euro Surveill. 2024;29(41); Kessel et al., Euro Surveill. 2024;29(5); Haller and Kleine, Hessisches Ärzteblatt 7-8/2025; ECDC Malaria AER 2022.

On 18 August, WIRED reported that Meta had run ads for Kromix, an app that turns a photograph of a real person into pornography. The Tech Transparency Project found them. One showed a woman resembling a prominent US politician, then the same face in a pornographic video. They were aimed at men only. Meta took them down after WIRED asked, and said most of that account’s ads had received 10 or fewer impressions.

Almost nobody. That cannot be tested. Meta counted impressions; its public archive publishes a different unit, an estimate of how many accounts in the EU saw an ad at least once. Meta prints that for every ad, including the ones it removes.

The Kromix ads carried a tagline: “Unleash Next-gen AI Magic”. Searching the ad library for that exact phrase returned, on 21 August, about 37,000 results by Meta’s own counter. We took the first 2,000 in Meta’s own ordering, most impressions first, and opened every one. They come from 999 pages, every one an unverified personal profile, and on 1,993 the audience Meta records is men.

Meta removed 1,624 of them and names the rule each broke: adult sexual exploitation (1,123), adult nudity and sexual activity (1,099), adult sexual solicitation (904), human exploitation (185), and on twenty, child sexual exploitation, abuse and nudity.

That name is nearly all that is left. Removal blanks the format, the title and the destination on 1,622 of them. The count stays: one estimate per ad, never a total, because one account may have been shown many. The lowest is 29, the largest 8,071. One that was live for 48 minutes reached 3,347.

The 376 Meta did not remove still show their fields: one title, one format, a link to an app install. Meta has named no rule on any of them, and 21 were still running when the record was taken on 21 August. By 25 August, 15 of those 21 were still up.

Sources: WIRED, Tech Transparency Project, Meta Ad Library, Meta Newsroom.
