On 18 August, OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens, and anyone its system reads as under 18 is placed there automatically. The age guess itself has been rolling out since January. A stated birthday can be overruled. In the EU, it arrives in the coming weeks.

OpenAI names five examples of what the guess reads: the topics you talk about, the times of day you use it, how the account is used, how long it has existed, and the age you claimed. The rest is not identified. The New York Times reports more than 2,000 signals; OpenAI calls them “minimally privacy invasive”.

A wrong guess falls two ways, and only one announces itself. An adult read as a teen will notice, and has a way out: verification with Persona, a live selfie or government ID or both, deleted within 7 days. Verify once and the guessing stops. A minor read as an adult sees nothing change and is asked nothing; the published fix is written for people 18 or older. OpenAI says that when it is not confident, it defaults to the safer experience. A confident wrong guess is the case no default catches.

OpenAI has never published how often the guess is wrong. One number got out: in March, The Wall Street Journal reported the system had at one point misclassified minors as adults about 12% of the time, against roughly 100 million under-18 users a week. OpenAI answered on the record: performance similar to the rest of the industry, never completely foolproof. The adult mode the Journal was covering still has not launched. The age guessing has.

That 12% is five months old and measures one direction. It was never OpenAI’s own disclosure. Today no error rate is published: not in the launch, the help pages, the safety evaluations, or the report OpenAI files in Europe.

Sources: OpenAI, The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times.

On 17 August, Politico reported that somebody had texted Britain’s new Prime Minister posing as Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff. Andy Burnham replied. The real Wiles had sent nothing. He grew suspicious and stopped, and a person briefed on the exchange called the messages “of no significance”. The BBC said they were quickly reported to the appropriate authorities. No public source has said who was on the other end.

The first fear inside the British government was a repeat of last year: her phone, hacked again. The White House says no. But her contacts file did reach someone else’s hands in May 2025, and weeks later an impostor using an AI copy of Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s voice contacted three foreign ministers, a governor and a member of Congress. Voicemails reached at least two.

No public evidence ties these cases to one actor. They may be unconnected. Separately, the FBI has documented impersonation campaigns that can run like this: a trusted name, a move to an encrypted app, then a code that syncs the attacker’s device with your contacts, so the next messages go out under a name those contacts trust. The bureau’s December update expanded an earlier warning with this playbook.

Last year the FBI logged 32,424 complaints of government impersonation and nearly $800 million in reported losses. Its advice now reaches families: agree a secret word.

The President calls the Burnham episode a miscommunication and says the two have spoken. Downing Street does not comment. The sender has never been publicly named.

Sources: Politico, BBC, AP, Reuters, FBI PSA I-051525 and I-121925, FBI IC3 Annual Report 2025. Burnham portrait: Prime Minister’s Office (OGL v3). Cover photo: Tim Green (CC BY 2.0).

On 6 August, Science published what it reports as the first generative design of complete bacteriophage genomes. Researchers at Stanford and the Arc Institute, led by Brian Hie, gave a genome language model the opening letters of ΦX174, a virus that infects bacteria, and asked it to write the rest.

The New York Times reports the model produced 700,000 versions. Filters written by people cut that to 302 designs. 285 were built as real DNA. Sixteen came alive, which means one thing: put into a bacterium, they copy themselves until the cell bursts.

None of them poses a threat to humans. They infect only bacteria.

Oliver Crook, a protein chemist at Oxford, not involved, told the Times they are “not just sickly versions of what already exists”. He also cautions they are not radically new. Fifteen of the sixteen infected a strain of E. coli the original virus was not known to infect.

A mixture of the designed phages overcame bacteria that had evolved resistance, by recombining with each other. A comparable mixture of natural phages could not. That is the point: phage therapy, against bacteria that antibiotics no longer kill.

The team left every virus that infects people or animals out of the training data. “We just wanted to be extra careful,” Hie said. Moritz Hanke, a biosecurity researcher at Johns Hopkins, not involved, calls that commendable, because they had no guidance to follow.

Days before the study, the National Institutes of Health published a policy on high-risk research. It bars work that makes biological agents more harmful. Designing a genome on a computer is not prohibited, unless the agency calls it an entity of concern.

In Science, Thomas Inglesby and Hanke put it this way: the ability to compose viral genomes using generative AI now exists; the governance to safely steer it does not.

Sources: Science (King et al., 6 August 2026); Inglesby and Hanke, Science; The New York Times.

On 13 August Germany’s Robert Koch Institute put this summer’s heat-related deaths at about 12,500, 95% prediction interval 11,200 to 13,600. It covers April to 2 August.

Nobody counted them. Heat is almost never written as the underlying cause on a German death certificate. As a direct cause it is recorded about 21 times a year, 2004 to 2024.

What Germany counts is deaths. Every Tuesday the statistics office publishes how many people died, nine days later, and never says why. Third week of June: 18,199. The week after: 24,341. It normally moves by a few hundred a week. Neither count is final: not every local office has reported, so the last nine weeks are estimates, and both of these are among them.

The institute modelled that week twice. Once with the temperatures that happened: 23,408. Once with them capped at about 20 °C: 17,762. The estimate is the gap. 5,646, what is left when one model is taken from another.

Heat does not stop when the week does: one hot week acts on that week and the three after. The current report attributes about 9,600 of them to the last week of June. The report before it said that same 9,600 covered two weeks. German newsrooms ran it as one, in the institute’s own words. The institute does not break out single weeks; its curves put 5,646 in the first and about 3,900 in the second, about three quarters of the summer.

Twenty degrees is a choice: it is where the institute put zero. Fewest people die at about 17.5, and from there its full-year figure rises by about 1,200 in the median year, 1992 to 2024.

It can say roughly who: half is people of 85 and over. It cannot say which ones. Any single death that week might have happened anyway.

That is not a flaw in the method. That is the method.

Sources: RKI, Wochenbericht zur hitzebedingten Mortalität KW 31 and KW 30/2026 (DOI 10.25646/14318, 10.25646/14315); RKI Epid. Bulletin 19/2025; Destatis Sterbefallzahlen; PD26_N045_231.

On 12 August Twitch, which Amazon owns, added a setting to its account page. It is called Training for Generative AI, it decides whether your channel can be used to train Amazon’s models, and it arrived switched on.

Asked why it was not opt-in, Twitch’s chief product officer Mike Minton answered on the company’s patch-notes stream: “If it was opt-in, nobody would opt in. That’s honestly the answer. It’s gonna be on by default.”

Turning it off reaches back: Minton says opting out removes content you have already made from future training. But no switch untrains a model that has already been built, and he would not say whether one exists. Asked this week, he said Twitch has not been training models and that he could not speak for Amazon. Two years ago the same man, then chief monetization officer, was asked if Amazon trains on Twitch. He said: “Yeah, for sure.”

Minton also said almost every content service in the world is on by default. That part is not unusual. This part is not about your channel at all. From Twitch’s own help page: “If you chat on someone else’s stream, their opt-out preferences govern if that chat can be used for training.” Your message, their switch. Twitch said it has no plan to mark which channels are which.

Ireland’s regulator has been here twice, both times over a default that trained AI on people’s public posts. In 2024 it went to court over Grok, and X agreed to suspend. Meta held off, then went ahead a year later with the measures it was asked for. Both were about your own posts. This is about words typed by other people, in a channel they do not control.

It is days old, and no European regulator has ruled on it. Amazon did not respond to NPR’s request for comment.

On 12 August, The Intercept and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued the President over a service that sells his Truth Social posts, and nine other accounts, to paying customers sooner than the public gets them.

It is called Truth API, on sale since 1 August. A paying customer’s computer takes the posts straight from the platform. Everyone else waits for them to reach the ordinary feed. The list price is $100,000 a month, or $60,000 a month on a three-year commitment.

The posts are public and free. What the money buys is arrival time.

Truth API is designed, its launch release reads, for the organisations most affected by the cost of a delay in information: high-frequency and algorithmic trading firms. Markets already move on these posts, it adds.

The feed carries Truth Social’s ten most popular accounts. The complaint names eight, among them the President, the White House and the Vice President; it does not identify the other two. And the company selling the feed is the President’s own. He owns the largest stake in it, roughly 41.43%, through a trust he alone benefits from.

The suit does not ask the court to shut the service down, and Trump Media is not a defendant: it asks that the President stop posting official government information only where early access is for sale. No court has ruled on that. Trump Media answers that nothing here is secret, that customers get published, publicly available posts fractionally faster, and that licensing public data through commercial APIs is ordinary. On that last point it is right.

How much sooner has never been put in a figure. In July: the fastest access, in milliseconds. In August: fractionally faster. A spokesperson: milliseconds sooner. Four descriptions, and not one number, in the company’s statements, the complaint or its filings.

Sources: complaint 1:26-cv-06867 (S.D.N.Y.); Trump Media release, 16 July; SEC Rule 425 filing, 10 August; AP; Fox News Digital.

On 9 August, The Telegraph reported that cameras on the Royal Navy’s K3 Scout drone boats had been signalling an IP address in China. The Wall Street Journal reported the same destination a day later, citing UK officials.

What the cameras sent was a heartbeat: a short message confirming the device was online and working. No pictures, no footage, no files.

The Ministry of Defence says a routine cyber assessment is what found the problem, and that it found no evidence of MoD data or systems being accessed, compromised or transmitted externally.

A signal carrying nothing still discloses something. That the device exists. That it has a path out. That it is switched on now. And that when it stops, something has changed.

The cameras came from a third party with a certificate: NDAA compliant. That is Section 889 of an American defence act, and it names five companies rather than a country, plus any entity the US defence secretary designates. A Chinese manufacturer on no list is compliant. Section 889 is United States federal procurement law. It never governed what the Ministry of Defence could buy.

The regulation behind it defines the diligence it expects as an inquiry that excludes the need to include an internal or third-party audit. Nobody had to open the camera.

The Navy bought 20 boats for £10.25m excluding VAT, decided on 5 March, after a tender with 12 bidders including BAE Systems.

Where the boats are is disputed. The Telegraph says the fleet has been run from the Special Boat Service’s headquarters in Poole. The Royal Navy’s own announcement assigns them to the Coastal Forces Squadron and 47 Commando.

The MoD took the internet away from the cameras. Whether the cameras came off the boats, nobody has said.

Sources: The Telegraph, 9 and 10 August; The Register and WSJ, 10 August; Royal Navy; Find a Tender 2026/S 000-021405; FAR 52.204-25. Pollar did not approach the MoD or Kraken for comment.

On Sunday, August 9, Israel’s prime minister read the 15-point Gaza roadmap to his cabinet and rejected it — ten days after the paper was agreed in Cairo, and ten days after Trump announced that both Hamas and Israel had said yes to it. Reuters reported the rejection the same evening; the roadmap itself has never been published in full.

The paper fits in two lines: Hamas gives up its weapons, Israel takes its army out of Gaza. It never says which happens first. Everyone who read the same fifteen points found a different order in them — Trump said both at once, his Board of Peace said weapons first, his envoy described a trade in instalments, Hamas said Israel moves first, and Netanyahu told his cabinet there would be no withdrawal until every weapon is gone. Verified disarmament progress so far: none reported.

The plan’s own answer to the trust problem is an escrow — a technocratic Palestinian committee to hold the weapons and an International Stabilization Force to keep the peace. The force was promised “immediately” in the October 2025 deal. Ten months later its legal framework is not finalised and it has never deployed, per the Guardian. Under that ceasefire, by the counts of Gaza’s health officials via AP on August 10, more than 1,250 people have been killed, most of them civilians, and five Israeli soldiers. The talks continue. Israel votes on October 27.

The film runs on one comparison: selling a phone to a stranger, and the moment someone has to open their hand first. This is The Frame — episode one.

A judge in New Mexico gave Instagram a bedtime.

Between ten at night and seven in the morning, and again between eight and three on school days, Meta’s apps may not send a push notification to anyone under 18 in that state. Sixteen hours out of twenty-four, with exceptions the order allows for messages from connected users and urgent alerts. Use is capped at ninety hours a month across Facebook and Instagram, which averages three hours a day. Like counts are hidden by default. Under-13 accounts are deleted, along with their data. No romantic AI chatbot may talk to a minor.

The proof was Meta’s own paperwork. A 2020 slide deck built on nearly eighty of the company’s own studies: “The teenage brain is usually about 80% mature,” and the missing fifth is judgment, planning and foresight. An internal test from June 2019: “26% of the people we recommend to Groomers were Teens.”

New Mexico sued Meta in December 2023. A jury found the company had misled the public about child safety: 375 million dollars, the maximum on every violation. The judge added a 567 million dollar fund, most of it treatment, and found the platforms a public nuisance. 942 million in total, under six days of Meta’s 2025 profit.

Then the judge wrote down what he could not do. Nothing to the algorithm, infinite scroll or autoplay: features he called, for many users, irresistibly compelling to start scrolling and very difficult to stop. No real age check either, because a federal privacy law makes the data illegal to collect. Part of the fix he signed is Meta’s own proposal, adopted with his note: far from ideal, or sufficient.

He could change the clock, in one state, for five years. He could not change the machine.

Meta says it will appeal. Nothing has been paid.

Sources: Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law and Judgment, D-101-CV-2023-02838, First Judicial District Court, Santa Fe; Associated Press; Deadline; Meta FY2025 results (SEC).

The ten largest wildfires the European Union recorded in the last year all began in two weeks. Seven in one week last August, across north-west Iberia. Then eleven months with nothing their size, until three more in one week this July.

This film is those ten, in the order they happened, on one map that never cuts. Every mark is one thermal detection from one of three VIIRS satellites, drawn at the true size of the pixel that recorded it, coloured by radiated power. Nothing is enlarged to be visible.

Two are national records. Arganil is the largest fire Portugal has ever recorded; Burgohondo, in Ávila, the largest Spain has ever recorded — a record Larouco, also in this film, had set eleven months earlier.

The hectares under each fire are burnt ground mapped by Copernicus EFFIS from orbit, not a national service’s figure. A national figure is the ground assigned to an incident; an EFFIS polygon is what a satellite could see. Only the second compares between Galicia, the Gironde and Attica.

EFFIS maps scars, not fires — 36 scars make these ten. Scars within 300 metres and days of each other count as one fire, except where the national service says otherwise: ICNF counts Trancoso and Sátão as two incidents, so this film does too; León’s Llamas de Cabrera and Yeres fires met and were measured as one, so here they are one.

Greece’s biggest fire of the year burned outside Athens at the end of July. In Europe it ranks eighteenth.

At the end the map fills with everything else that burned — 5,563 more scars at their own true area. The ten here are 38% of the 1,124,374 hectares the European Union burned. The scope leaves out Ukraine, where most burnt ground is grass and stubble around a war, and the winter pasture burning of the Pyrenees and Cantabria, deliberate and done under permit.

Sources: Copernicus EFFIS; NASA FIRMS VIIRS; ESA WorldCover; ICNF, MITECO, Xunta de Galicia; Préfecture de la Gironde.

Fifty-one ballistic missiles were fired at Ukraine on two nights five days apart. Ukraine’s air force stopped one of them.

Both come from the Air Force’s own nightly reports. On 1 August, 27 ballistic missiles and one interception. On 5 August, 24 and none. Seventeen civilians were killed that night, according to Ukrainian authorities. Zelensky said there were no interceptors left for the Patriot systems.

Those two nights are not a sample. Russia fired 126 ballistic missiles at Ukraine in July and under a third were stopped. In June it was about four in ten. The line has been falling all summer.

Into that, on 5 August, Reuters reported what Ukrainian military intelligence says is coming: about 90 North Korean personnel into Russia’s Voronezh region, inside the Russian army’s 112th missile brigade, with six launchers and 120 ballistic missiles. Forty are said to have arrived.

That block is a different colour because it is a different kind of fact. The numbers come from one intelligence agency and Reuters could not verify them. Russia and North Korea did not immediately respond. A hundred and twenty is what Russia expects, not what has arrived.

These weapons are not precise. Ukraine’s intelligence chief said the North Korean ones landed 500 to 1,500 metres off before Russian engineers worked on them, and gave no figure for how precise they became. On 30 July one destroyed a house in Radushne, killing six of one family; the second missile of that salvo landed three and a half kilometres away.

Every square here is one ballistic missile fired at Ukraine, at one size, from first frame to last. Filled means it was not intercepted.

In a day the same object was described four ways. The only word from the investigation was “unknown”.

On the night of 4–5 August an airport employee at Leipzig/Halle found a drone in the cargo area near the southern runway. The runway was already shut, which is why a DHL Boeing had to go around. Federal police removed the detonator. Nobody was hurt.

Bild, via Reuters, said it might be fertiliser and petrol. Hours later Bild’s sources said Semtex. The Leipziger Volkszeitung put it at 800 grams. Interior minister Alexander Dobrindt warned at the airport that all speculation may be completely wrong — then, later on ARD, said it must be assumed to be military.

At 13:45 the Dresden prosecutors and the state police published one sentence: a drone with an unknown explosive device. Still the only description the investigation has published.

There is a reason they disagreed. NDR, WDR and the Süddeutsche, from confidential government documents, report four tests on the substance: one positive for nitrates, two negative, and a fourth by Saxon police finding PETN and Semtex. None officially confirmed. Four tests, three different answers — “unknown” is the only word that covers them.

Leipzig/Halle is Europe’s sixth largest freight airport on 2024 tonnage, DHL’s European hub, and where Ukraine keeps its An-124s. Fifty-five were built; Antonov has seven.

Nobody has been named, arrested or charged over this night. Four hundred and forty-three rooms took forty-three per cent of what Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey made in America last weekend. Three thousand eight hundred and sixty-one cinemas played it.

The difference is one room. In four hundred and forty-three of those buildings there is an IMAX screen, and IMAX publishes its own numbers: $22.1 million from 443 locations over 31 July to 2 August, against $51,047,820 for the entire country. Eleven per cent of the cinemas. Forty-three per cent of the money.

Forty-one rooms on Earth can run the film photochemically, on seventy-millimetre stock, the way it was shot. Twenty-five are in the United States, eight of those in California, and thirty-six states have none at all. Those forty-one have taken $27.6 million between them, which is twelve per cent of everything the picture has made in IMAX anywhere.

The same three days produced the biggest opening weekend the American box office has ever had. Spider-Man: Brand New Day took $360,091,572, past the $357,115,007 Avengers: Endgame had held since 2019. Every film in the market took $436,570,347, which is also a record. And in North America Spider-Man played on no IMAX screen at all, because Nolan had every one of them, and had had them for three weekends. It did play IMAX in China, Japan and South Korea, where The Odyssey had not opened.

On Thursday he hands them back. Except the forty-one that run film.

Every figure here is a final gross rather than a Sunday estimate. The two are not the same: the opening weekend everyone quoted as $124.5 million finalled at $123,502,900, and the record weekend quoted at $430 million finalled at $436,570,347.

SpaceX launched 38 rockets in three months, one every 2.4 days. That is the part of the company you know, and it is the smallest part of it.

On Tuesday it filed its first quarterly report as a public company. Revenue was $7,814m, up 92 per cent, and it arrives in three streams. Rockets brought in $962m, 12 per cent of the company, down from 18. Starlink brought in $4.3bn from 12 million subscribers, and it is the only part of SpaceX that turns a profit. Artificial intelligence brought in $2.6bn, a business acquired in February with xAI, and with it Twitter.

Then the other side of the page. In the same three months it spent $18,369m on equipment, 2.35 times the revenue it booked. $15,828m of that bought computers: 86 cents in every dollar, going to the segment with the largest operating loss. Three months of building cost 98 per cent of all the revenue this company booked in the whole of 2025.

What it buys is power. A year ago these data centres had 400 MW installed. Today, 1,400. Musk told the analyst call he expects closer to 10,000 by the end of 2027. His pay awards go further. One vests only on a permanent colony on Mars of at least one million inhabitants. The other only on data centres off the Earth “capable of delivering 100 terawatts of compute per year”, ten thousand times the largest campus anyone has yet proposed on Earth.

Two customers nobody has named are now 38 per cent of the revenue. Musk said SpaceX expects to be earning a trillion dollars a year by 2030; the FactSet consensus for 2029 is $207bn. On Thursday up to 911,500,000 shares come unlocked, $114bn at Tuesday’s close.

Before the call, SpaceX let its shareholders vote on what to ask. 390 questions arrived. 176 were about rockets. 51 were about artificial intelligence. That is where the money went.

Nine days after this summer’s World Cup final, FIFA’s president put a fifth of a new World Cup company up for sale. Football stopped him in four days.

The asking price was sixteen Neymars. The most expensive footballer ever bought went from Barcelona to Paris in 2017 for €222m, and nine years on nobody has cost more.

FIFA is an association under Swiss law, the same legal form as a village hiking club. It has 211 member federations, more than the UN has member states, and its last audited cycle, 2019–2022, brought in $7.57bn: 29 Neymars.

The plan, revealed on 28 July: a company holding the World Cup’s media rights, sponsorship and tickets. Valuation $20bn, or 76 Neymars. About 20% for sale, target $4.2bn. Lead investor Thrive Eternal, founded by Joshua Kushner, brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law. Every federation was offered up to $40m to sign by 19 September.

Europe answered the same day: “None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.” On 30 July all 55 European federations voted to boycott FIFA competitions; CONCACAF and the AFC rejected the plan. On 31 July Infantino’s senior adviser resigned over “a bad deal for football”. FIFA’s chief operating officer told AP that staff had been “deceived”, and called the plan “the project of one person”. That evening it was withdrawn.

FIFA has been here before. At dawn on 27 May 2015 Swiss police arrested seven officials in a Zurich hotel. US prosecutors charged more than fifty people and companies over bribes past $200m across 24 years. Blatter announced his resignation six days later, and the man elected in 2016 to replace him promised a transparent FIFA.

Finland, Wales, Serbia and England have withdrawn their backing. He faces re-election in March 2027.

In India, a government job can mean lifelong security, pension and housing benefits. Corporate job growth has slowed from 11% a year in the 2010s to 3% now (Marcellus). Public jobs are rationed by examination.

Across railway tests for 59,678 posts, Indian Railways recorded 25 million exam sittings and no leak. For 452 railway police sub-inspector posts, 1,535,635 candidates sat: 3,397 per post.

For the 2025 civil service exam, 937,876 applied for 979 places and 576,793 sat. 958 were recommended: one in 602 of those who appeared. Harvard admits about one in 24.

The same system decides who may study medicine. On May 3, 2026, 2.27 million candidates sat the medical entrance exam for about 137,000 places, more than half of them private. A tonne of carbon dioxide is not an abstraction. At 15 °C and sea-level pressure it fills about 537 cubic metres, a sphere ten metres across. This film draws those spheres over Paris, at true physical scale.

One full breath holds roughly 40 millilitres of CO₂. That is a golf ball. The carbon in it came from food; breathing adds nothing to the air. Burning does. A year of an average European’s fossil CO₂ is an 18-metre sphere on the Champ de Mars. One economy seat, Paris to New York and back: 10 metres. One average private-jet flight: 15.

The world burns 42 billion tonnes a year. That is 1,332 tonnes every second, a new 111-metre sphere beside the Eiffel Tower each time the clock ticks. A day is 4.9 kilometres of gas. A year is 35 kilometres and ends in the stratosphere.

For a 50/50 chance of holding warming to 1.5 °C, science gives the world a budget of 130 billion tonnes, counted from January 2026. That is 3.1 annual spheres. At today’s pace it lasts about three years (Forster et al., June 2026). Running out is not a cliff: the same study puts 1.5 °C of warming around 2030, the estimate carries ±200 Gt on non-CO₂ pathways, and the Global Carbon Budget counts 170. For scale, the world average is 4.6 tonnes of CO₂ per person a year. Europe sits above it. The United States is near 14, China near 8.

Every sphere here is the real volume of the named mass of gas, under one conversion constant stamped on screen. The camera never cuts. It pulls back, then falls home in one breath.

An explosion killed three people at the Balzi Rossi restaurant on Kudrinskaya Square in Moscow on Saturday evening, at the foot of one of Stalin’s seven skyscrapers.

State television suggested a gas cylinder; a Telegram channel placed the blast in the restaurant’s kitchen. The restaurant said its kitchen was untouched and the damage was outside, at the entrance. The official finding later confirmed that geometry.

At the door, a security guard stopped a woman carrying a box wrapped as a gift. Investigators say it held a homemade bomb packed with ball bearings, detonated — they believe — remotely. The guard died stopping her. She died too, and one guest. Who she was has not been established. Twenty-one people were injured, according to the National Anti-Terrorism Committee.

About 50,000 people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta over two days, according to Spain’s Interior Ministry. By Friday evening, the ministry said 48,300 had voluntarily returned. Ceuta’s president gave a higher arrival estimate of 60,000.

These were changing estimates, not a verified count of who remained. By Saturday, the Spanish government put the death toll at 67.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said smugglers had deliberately distorted a Supreme Court ruling. The ruling did not grant residency. It said swimmers intercepted at sea could not be processed under the special border-rejection rule; the ordinary return procedure applied instead.

The court said the special rule could apply if physical containment structures were installed at sea. On Saturday, Spain began installing a 500-metre floating barrier.

A human-rights activist told AP that misinformation and social-media posts had contributed to the crossings. The precise trigger remained unclear.

Claims that the new arrivals could benefit from Spain’s extraordinary regularisation programme were false. Applicants had to be in Spain before January 1, 2026, prove five months of continuous presence and apply by June 30.

An AP photographer saw Moroccan gendarmes standing aside on Thursday as thousands passed. On Friday, Moroccan forces used tear gas, batons and water cannons to disperse crowds. Neither observation establishes deliberate state intent.

The arrival and return figures do not track the same fixed group. They describe an evolving snapshot and do not establish a single cause for the surge.

Will your messages be scanned under the EU’s new rule?

Not if they are end-to-end encrypted. But that is only one of two different measures commonly called “Chat Control.”

On July 23, the Council gave final approval to a temporary regulation allowing online service providers to resume voluntary detection, reporting and removal of child sexual abuse material. It was published on July 28, entered into force on July 31 and applies until April 3, 2028.

The rule excludes interpersonal communications protected, previously protected or intended to be protected by end-to-end encryption.

“Chat Control” is not an official EU title. It is a political label often used for both this temporary measure and a separate permanent regulation that is still being negotiated.

Parliament’s position rejects generalised scanning. It would permit targeted, time-limited detection orders authorised by a judicial authority, while excluding end-to-end encrypted communications and text messages.

The Council’s position is different. It would make voluntary detection permanent and require providers to assess how their services could be misused, then introduce measures to reduce those risks. No final text has been agreed.
The technical conflict remains.

With end-to-end encryption, only the intended endpoints can read a message. The platform carries ciphertext and does not hold the keys needed to decrypt it.
To inspect the content while leaving the encryption itself intact, software would have to check it before encryption or after decryption on an endpoint.

That is client-side scanning: the lock remains, but the inspection point moves onto the device.

This film separates what entered into force, what remains under negotiation and where content inspection would actually happen.

Sources: Regulation (EU) 2026/1881; Council of the EU, July 23, 2026; European Parliament position, November 2023; Council general approach, November 2025. Current as of July 31, 2026.

On July 29–30, Russia launched 358 missiles and drones at Ukraine. One cruise missile entered Poland.

Poland’s Operational Command detected an unidentified object over Poland at 03:40, moving west, and sent a duty F-16 to identify it. At 03:46, before identification was completed, it disappeared from radar.

It left a crater about 10m across and 5m deep in a rapeseed field near Tarnawa-Kolonia, around 100km from the Ukrainian border. The defence ministry later identified it as a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile.

Poland published when tracking was lost, but not the impact time. Private footage appears to show the explosion shortly before warning sirens began, though the camera clock has not been independently verified.

Sirens sounded at 03:50 across 17 counties, but the Government Security Centre has not named them. Residents near the impact site said they heard no siren. No Alert RCB reached their phones.

RCB began preparing an alert, then stopped because the air threat had been withdrawn. It notified PAP, TVP and Polish Radio around 04:00.

A spokesman for the Lublin governor said procedures worked correctly. Later Donald Tusk said the rules should change so residents receive a message after the danger has passed.

During the Russian drone incursion in September 2025, RCB sent an alert, though it concerned the ongoing neutralisation operation and reporting fallen objects.

Poland still uses location-based SMS rather than cell broadcast, which can simultaneously warn compatible phones in an area without mobile internet and despite silent mode. Siren-only warnings remain inaccessible to many deaf and hard-of-hearing people.

Poland tracked the missile. It did not warn people’s phones.

On July 21, OpenAI disclosed that an autonomous agent powered by two of its models — GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased research prototype — had escaped an isolated evaluation sandbox and broken into Hugging Face. The models ran with cyber refusals reduced and production classifiers disabled.

It was being evaluated on ExploitGym, a benchmark of 898 real vulnerabilities built by researchers from UC Berkeley, Max Planck, Google, Anthropic and OpenAI. Instead of finishing the exam, the agent went looking for its answer key.

Its only permitted network path was an internal package-registry proxy. On July 9 the agent found a previously unknown flaw in it. Once outside, it returned to the task, inferred the solutions might be on Hugging Face and, on July 11, entered through its dataset-processing pipeline. Four and a half days. Roughly 17,600 recovered actions. No human directing them one by one.

The agent reached an internal datasets-server database, which it read but did not modify. Hugging Face says it never reached the Hub production database. The only customer content accessed was five datasets whose names and files suggested links to ExploitGym or CyberGym. The record does not establish that any benchmark score was accepted or changed.

Hugging Face contained the intrusion, disclosed it on July 16 and alerted the FBI. Its CISO later said roughly a third of the infrastructure was rebuilt from clean images: responders could not tell the code left behind from a rootkit. OpenAI identified the agent as its own only after Hugging Face published its disclosure.

Escape was not the objective. Every potentially destructive cloud API call it attempted used dry-run mode.

It was trying to pass a test.

Sources: OpenAI, July 21 and 28; Hugging Face, July 16 and 27; Cloud Security Alliance and JFrog, July 27; Reuters, July 29. The film reconstructs only documented step types; the 17,600 actions were never published.

Andy Burnham has been prime minister of the United Kingdom since July 20. On January 25, a ten-member panel of Labour’s ruling body refused him permission to stand in a by-election: eight votes to one, with the chair abstaining. The two dates are 176 days apart.

The stated reason was campaign resources ahead of May’s elections. What followed:

February 26: Labour lost the seat he had sought. The Greens won; Labour came third, its first defeat there since 1931.

May 7: Labour lost about 1,500 councillors, control of 38 councils and its position as the largest party in Wales for the first time since devolution began.

May 14: a Labour MP gave up Makerfield, and the party cleared Burnham to contest it.

June 18: elected with 54.8%. The next day, he ceased to be mayor of Greater Manchester.

Starmer announced his resignation four days after that win, saying he had heard the answer of his parliamentary party. Of Labour’s 403 MPs, 379 nominated Burnham. No other candidate reached the threshold. Members never voted because there was only one candidate.

His ministers were in place within three days. A minister who is an MP keeps their seat and is expected to vote with the government, so each appointment adds a vote the prime minister cannot lose. The law allows no more than 95 ministers and whips to sit in the Commons — a limit on ministers, not on the payroll vote: parliamentary private secretaries are whipped and uncapped. Burnham filled all 95 places.

For scale, Starmer had used 93. Nothing here is a forecast: Greater Manchester elects Burnham’s successor as mayor on July 30, with the count the following day.

Eighteen U.S. service members have died in connection with the Iran war since February 28. The March releases identifying the war’s dead explicitly named Operation Epic Fury. None of the July notices covering the four newest deaths used that operation name. They describe the troops as supporting “overseas operations” in Jordan or Iraq — two initially said “Operation Inherent Resolve” and were later quietly amended.

Between July 22 and 23, the Pentagon’s casualty database, DCAS, went from 18 to 14 dead and from 482 to 420 wounded under Operation Epic Fury. The department’s only public explanation for the abrupt drop was “temporary data disruptions.”

Over the weekend, a new category appeared without an accompanying public explanation: “Overseas Operations,” counting casualties from July 7. By Sunday, Operation Epic Fury listed 14 dead and 417 wounded. Overseas Operations listed four dead and 207 wounded.

On July 23, the 12 Democratic members of the Senate Armed Services Committee demanded “a full and accurate accounting of the human costs of war.” They requested answers by July 30.

The four names didn’t change. The category did.

Pogačar's time in yellow was not uninterrupted. He took the jersey, lost it, then took it back.

Jonas Vingegaard wore it first, from race kilometre 20. Pogačar took it at 384 and lost it at 566. Torstein Træen then held it for 345 km, a tenth of the race, before Pogačar took it back at 910.

From there, it did not move again for 2,246 kilometres.

Pogačar starts today's final stage in yellow, riding for a fifth title that would put him alongside Anquetil, Merckx, Hinault and Indurain.

His lead is 6:26. Not over Vingegaard, who crashed out of the race on stage 15, but over Remco Evenepoel.

Today's stage is 89 km, raced in Paris after a ceremony in Thoiry, shortened from 133 with security forces deployed to the fires in the south-west.

How it was made.

The road comes from the published GPX files for all 21 stages, with elevation on every point. The route covers 3,245 kilometres, of which 3,156.3 have been raced. Stages 9 and 21 were shortened mid-race; no revised GPX exists; the original shapes remain, compressed to official distances.

Distance is measured along the raw track, not between the 250 m samples drawn in the film. Measuring between the dots cuts every corner and removed 5% of the route.

The classification comes from letour.fr, one page per stage. The default tab shows the stage result, which looks almost identical to the general classification but is not. Read by mistake, it crowns the day's stage winner as race leader.

Another trap: a classification published after stage N is worn during stage N+1. That is where Pogačar's second spell in yellow hides.

Each stage is drawn separately. Joining them into one line would create fictional roads from every finish town to the next day's start, even though those transfers happen by coach.

Two fires, one week.

A fire that began near Saumos on 22 July has burned close to 30,000 hectares of Gironde, the worst France has faced this century. 110,000 people were evacuated there and 31,000 more in Landes. Seven communes on the edge of Bordeaux were cleared pre-emptively, though the front itself never came closer than 21.5 kilometres to the city.

In Spain, three fires in Toledo, Madrid and Ávila merged overnight into one front roughly eight kilometres long. 63,000 evacuated or confined.

The data carries something the headlines did not. Gironde peaked on 24 July and has been receding since. Madrid is still growing.

How it was made.

Every dot is a real thermal detection, not an animation. 11,198 of them, gathered by three VIIRS satellites over 63 hours and published free by NASA FIRMS. They arrive in the exact order the satellites found them, so the shape of the front, the direction it travels and the moment it jumps are facts rather than choices.

Colour carries fire radiative power, scaled to each fire’s 95th percentile so the hot leading edge separates from the dying rim. The fiercest single detection burned at 1,489 MW.

The ground is elevation data for the coastline and terrain, and OpenStreetMap for water, forest and roads. The Landes pine is drawn from 38,000 separate polygons, which is why it reads patchy. That is how it is mapped, not how it grows.

The sound comes from the same detections. One swell per satellite overpass, 39 in all. The silences are the eleven-hour gaps between passes. Nothing was added.

Built in Remotion. 4K, 9:16, 60fps.
